content: Discussion thread for #announce > M2F and ReasBook: a book-scale autoformalization

Tao's Analysis I has a human formalization (by Terry and contributors) -- I'm curious to ask if you've tried autoformalizing that itself already, and if so if anything interesting can be said about how the autoformalization compares to a "well designed" human one. (I'm not aware of other cases of full textbook formalization but if there are others I think it'd be interesting to ask the same question about those as well).

We noticed that Analysis I has already been fully human-formalized, so we have not tried autoformalizing it. You may take a look at the Lean source code in ReasBook to compare how our approach differs from the human formalization.
I feel like that it is human formalized is more reason to try it out, as you actually have a human baseline for comparison.
I couldn’t find estimates on compute/cost per page on average (though this might be user error). Could you share those?
Are there concrete numbers / results on the faithfulness between the informal statements and the Lean statements? I did not find them during my skim, but I might have missed it.

Matthew Ballard 发言道：

I couldn’t find estimates on compute/cost per page on average (though this might be user error). Could you share those?

For Terence Tao’s Analysis II (2022), our end-to-end run used about 210M model tokens in total.

Franz Huschenbeth 发言道：

Are there concrete numbers / results on the faithfulness between the informal statements and the Lean statements? I did not find them during my skim, but I might have missed it.

We recruited students to review the generated Lean statements against the original informal statements for faithfulness. Up to now, we have not found any cases where the Lean statement was unfaithful to the source text.

Chris Henson 发言道：

I feel like that it is human formalized is more reason to try it out, as you actually have a human baseline for comparison.

Sounds good — having a human baseline is a strong reason. We’ll add Analysis I to our roadmap and report back once we have a meaningful comparison.

Zichen Wang said:

Matthew Ballard 发言道：

I couldn’t find estimates on compute/cost per page on average (though this might be user error). Could you share those?

For Terence Tao’s Analysis II (2022), our end-to-end run used about 210M model tokens in total.

I'd also be curious about the compute costs for running Lean itself during a book formalization (i.e. across all tool use).

No problem. For Tao Analysis II, I computed Lean runtime across all recorded tool use:

  • Total Lean wall-time (lower bound): 94,553 s ≈ 26.3 h
  • Breakdown:
    • lean_check: 49,224.5 s ≈ 13.7 h
    • Agent Lean calls (subtotal): 45,329.0 s ≈ 12.6 h
      • lean-lsp.*: 19,687.0 s over 7,765 calls
      • lake env lean: 25,642.0 s over 4,201 calls

50years after automath. Landau's "Grundlagen" would be an obvious one:
https://pure.tue.nl/ws/files/1710991/23183.pdf

Bas Spitters said:

50years after automath. Landau's "Grundlagen" would be an obvious one:
https://pure.tue.nl/ws/files/1710991/23183.pdf

God! I never know that it was a concept 50 years ago!

I feel like that it is human formalized is more reason to try it out, as you actually have a human baseline for comparison.

Sadly it wont make for a good comparison, because frontier LLMs are likely already trained on Tao's companion (it has been on github since last summer), and probably will regurgitate the existing formalization.

I am very interested in running this for a Linear Algebra and Abstract Algebra textbooks, what would be the prerequisite resources? I have a long running vm on digital ocean and claude max subscription.

Impressive work! Has M2F been tested on FATE-X yet? Recall that Seed-Prover 1.5 reported 33% solved.
Also it seems the paper doesn't explain what PSR is, though the repo indicated it stands for "pass success rate".
